Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others
Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
There is something about me that made the event happen

vignette: José, a 53-year-old Latin American man and divorced tax consultant, has been struggling with the aftermath of an encounter with police violence that occurred two years ago. The traumatic event itself is still vivid in his mind: he was on his way to a client meeting when he witnessed a young man being unjustly beaten by several officers. The visible injuries and wounds on the victim were severe, leaving José feeling helpless and deeply disturbed. Since then, visual triggers like seeing injuries or pain in others have been overwhelming for him. A recent incident at work where he saw a colleague with an arm bandaged up sent him into a state of panic. He had come to believe that such reminders of victims are everywhere, and this has led José to feel deeply isolated from others. His fear is not just about the immediate danger but also about how others might perceive him if they knew what happened. José’s sense of isolation grew as he became more convinced that his life was no longer worth living, compounded by a belief that there is something inherently wrong with him that made the event happen. These negative appraisals have fueled his heightened state of threat monitoring and avoidance behaviors. He now avoids going to unfamiliar places because he feels unable to assess the danger accurately. His constant need for reassurance manifests in frequent checks behind him to ensure no one is following him, and a compulsion to identify escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere. For instance, when attending mandatory meetings at different locations, José spends considerable time identifying exits and assessing potential dangers. This behavior has led to his colleagues noticing an unusual level of anxiety, which further reinforces his belief that he is set apart from others. The cycle becomes increasingly self-reinforcing: the more José feels threatened by unfamiliar places and reminders of victims, the stronger his negative appraisals become. He believes that if he had been more vigilant or taken better precautions, perhaps nothing would have happened. This heightened sense of threat then leads to a constant state of alertness and further avoidance behaviors. José’s work as a tax consultant has been affected by these symptoms. His frequent absences due to panic attacks and his reluctance to travel for meetings have strained relationships with both clients and colleagues. The occupational strain adds to his feeling that he is not living up to his potential, deepening his sense of isolation and worthlessness. What finally brought José to seek help was a recent incident where he almost had a panic attack in front of an important client, leading him to cancel the meeting abruptly. He was certain that this pattern would only worsen if left unchecked. José is most afraid of losing his job and feeling completely isolated from society. However, he is also hoping for relief from these overwhelming fears and a return to a sense of normalcy in his life. Through therapy, José hopes to understand the connection between his traumatic experience and the subsequent symptoms that have taken over his daily functioning. He is eager to regain control and find ways to cope with his triggers without feeling so overwhelmed by fear and isolation.
